claims.text: Single-crystalline <110>-oriented CoCrFeNi nanopillars exhibit unusually high room-temperature uniform elongation while sustaining high flow stress.
The <110> orientation favors deformation twinning in CoCrFeNi nanopillars relative to orientations favoring pure slip.
Atomic-scale chemical compositional heterogeneity in CoCrFeNi produces spatial variations in local generalized stacking-fault energy.
The local generalized stacking-fault-energy variations are greater in <110>-oriented nanopillars than in baseline orientations favoring pure slip.
Wide local fault-energy variations promote joint or sequential activation of deformation twinning and dislocation slip.
Coordinated twinning and dislocation slip spatially delocalize deformation.
Deformation delocalization caused by coordinated twinning and slip delays necking failure.
Delayed necking caused by coordinated twinning and slip produces enhanced uniform tensile ductility.
Coordinated twinning and slip improve ductility while maintaining high strength.
Compared with other crystallographic orientations, <110>-oriented CoCrFeNi nanopillars have superior uniform elongation and high strength.
Baseline orientations with more uniform fault energies primarily deform by pure dislocation slip.
Pure-slip baseline orientations have lower ductility than <110>-oriented nanopillars.
Pure-slip baseline orientations exhibit less twinning–dislocation synergy than <110>-oriented nanopillars.
Computational modeling or high-resolution spectroscopic mapping can quantitatively determine local generalized stacking-fault-energy distributions in the tested nanopillars.
The controlled comparison requires single-crystalline CoCrFeNi nanopillars with identical composition and processing, differing in crystallographic orientation.
The initial nanopillars have minimal pre-existing defects.
The proposed mechanism is scoped to single-crystalline CoCrFeNi nanopillars tested in uniaxial tension at room temperature.
Applicability of the proposed mechanism to polycrystalline materials or other temperatures may be limited.
Failure of <110>-oriented nanopillars to show higher elongation together with greater fault-energy variation and coordinated twin–dislocation activity would falsify the hypothesis.
